pr_body:
Closes #103111

Relates to #81500. cc @tannergooding - hopefully this doesn't tread on any prior work.

This implements `IUtf8SpanParsable` on `IPAddress` and `IPNetwork`. It does so by making `IPAddressParser` generic between `byte` and `char`. Doing so needed deeper changes than I'd have liked (the separators aren't considered constants, which means that I had to swap a switch statement and its "goto case" statements for a set of if statements) As I did that, I replaced most of the unsafe code and pointers with `ReadOnlySpan`s (which eliminates a pattern where downstream code was pinning an ROS and passing its pointer.)

`IPAddressParser`, `IPv4AddressHelper` and `IPv6AddressHelper` are shared with System.Net.Quic, System.Net.Security and System.Private.Uri. The changes to the first two projects are pretty minor, consisting of one change to `TargetHostNameHelper`. System.Private.Uri is similar, but it makes more extensive use of pointers.

There are two differences between this PR and the underlying issue:
* I've added the public methods `Parse(ReadOnlySpan<byte>)` and `TryParse(ReadOnlySpan<byte>, out IPNetwork)` to `IPNetwork`.
* `IPNetwork` implements `IUtf8SpanParsable` explicitly rather than implicitly.

In both cases, this is done to maintain consistency with the `ISpanParsable` members which were already implemented. I've taken this to be covered by the original API review.

It's worth noting that `IPv6AddressHelper<TChar>.IsValid` in System.Private.Uri continues to reference `char*` rather than `ReadOnlySpan<TChar>`. This is inconsistent, but I've left it alone for now. I'd prefer to address that in a follow-up PR which replaces the unsafe components from `Uri.PrivateParseMinimal` and the methods it calls with a ROS.

Note regarding the `new-api-needs-documentation` label:

    This serves as a reminder for when your PR is modifying a ref *.cs file and adding/modifying public APIs, please make sure the API implementation in the src *.cs file is documented with triple slash comments, so the PR reviewers can sign off that change.

Hi @edwardneal, sorry for the delay in getting to this, I had missed the tag initially since this is under the networking area.

It's worth noting that `IPAddress` and `IPNetwork` are not part of APIs that https://github.com/dotnet/runtime/issues/81500 was approved for, and so before this can move forward there needs to be a new API proposal that specifically asks for implementing `IUtf8SpanParsable` on these types.

That proposal should be straightforward and I expect have no issues going through API review, at which point this can likely get merged. If you could assist in opening such a proposal, that should help the process go along faster.

Thanks @tannergooding. Sorry for the confusion here - I read the original issue as approving the addition of `IUtf8SpanParsable` and `IUtf8SpanFormattable` to anything already implementing `ISpanFormattable`, and `IPAddress` and `IPNetwork` both do so. Should I just raise the API proposal for the additional  `IPNetwork.Parse(ReadOnlySpan<byte>)` and `IPNetwork.TryParse(ReadOnlySpan<byte>, out IPNetwork)` methods and `IPNetwork`'s explicit interface implementation, or should I also include `IPAddress` in that?

> should I also include IPAddress in that?

We want to include all new public APIs and interfaces in the proposal whether that is for `IUtf8SpanParsable`, `IUtf8SpanFormattable`, or both; as well as any overloads beyond this.

> I read the original issue as approving the addition of IUtf8SpanParsable and IUtf8SpanFormattable to anything already implementing ISpanFormattable

The general spirit behind the feature fits that, but we still do explicit review and sign-off as there are often edge cases that we may warrant different consideration.
Given that we are blocked on API review, I would recommend to either change the PR to Draft or close it, until the API is approved. @edwardneal what do you prefer and can you please do it? Thanks!

I've adjusted the API surface following the review yesterday. There's still an open question for review: is threading the char/byte generics through all of `IPAddressParser` and its dependencies the right way to proceed, or would it be less risky for IPAddress/IPNetwork to simply call Encoding.UTF8.GetChars on the UTF8 input and passing through to ISpanParsable<T>.Parse? This would leave the underlying IP address parsing as char-only, but there'd be no impact on Uri or System.Net.Quic.

Thanks @MihaZupan. I agree with all (bar one or two) of your points, will resolve them shortly.

I started to use `TChar.CreateTruncating('x')` in various places throughout the parsing logic, but found that it quickly became harder to keep track of, (and they didn't behave as I wanted them to) so I refactored them into constant-value fields. I can't quite make them compiler constants, but making them static & readonly comes as close as I can - hopefully enough for the JIT to treat them similarly, and I expect them to perform (very marginally) better than calling `TChar.CreateTruncating` multiple times per method call.

A class-scoped field of type `TChar` in turn requires the `IPAddressParser` class to be made generic... but this also centralises the (slightly awkward) type constraints which are needed on almost every method in the class anyway. The cost is that I have to explicitly specify the `TChar` type at every call site - but there are only a few call sites.

Do the constants harm readability, and could I simply rename them instead of making `IPAddressParser` non-generic?

> making them static & readonly comes as close as I can - hopefully enough for the JIT to treat them similarly, and I expect them to perform (very marginally) better than calling TChar.CreateTruncating multiple times per method call

Unfortunately, NativeAOT might not preinitialize these, inserting cctor checks and calls into the parsing code, then dereferencing these instead of having them to be constants. I know there have been improvements in that area but it's not guaranteed last time I checked.

> and I expect them to perform (very marginally) better than calling TChar.CreateTruncating multiple times per method call.

Things like `TChar.CreateTruncating` / `CreateChecked` should be entirely optimized out - they shouldn't be actual calls in generated code (casting a byte to a char, or a char to a char can't overflow => no-op).
Small nit: I'd prefer `CreateChecked` over `Truncating` since all you're really doing is casting the `TChar` without the intent to change its value (and checked is slightly shorter).

> A class-scoped field of type TChar in turn requires the IPAddressParser class to be made generic... but this also centralises the (slightly awkward) type constraints which are needed on almost every method in the class anyway.

But there's also a bunch of helpers there that aren't doing anything generic (e.g. everything in Uri).
Making the class generic forces all of those to also be generic.
There aren't that many places that'd need the `where TChar : unmanaged, IBinaryInteger<TChar>` suffix, my preference would be to switch to that.

> Do the constants harm readability, and could I simply rename them instead of making IPAddressParser non-generic?

If the class itself isn't generic this is sort of a moot point, but IMO names like `ComponentSeparator` hurt readability over something like `Space`, `Colon`, `Dot`.

> Things like `TChar.CreateTruncating` / `CreateChecked` should be entirely optimized out - they shouldn't be actual calls in generated code (casting a byte to a char, or a char to a char can't overflow => no-op).

That was my only major reservation with performance. We can guarantee that it'll only ever be called with bytes and chars and as such we can be certain that the return values are always going to be constant... but the compiler has no way to know that. I wasn't sure if the JIT did, so wanted to protect against the case where it didn't with a static readonly variable.

I don't personally agree with variable naming - a variable named `ComponentSeparator` is clearly the separator between components of an IP address, while one named `Colon` or `Dot` doesn't communicate what it's used for. It's not a blocking point though, and there's no performance reason for those constant-value variables to be stored at the class level; I'll pull them down to the functions and make the class non-generic.

> Things like TChar.CreateTruncating / CreateChecked should be entirely optimized out - they shouldn't be actual calls in generated code (casting a byte to a char, or a char to a char can't overflow => no-op).
Small nit: I'd prefer CreateChecked over Truncating since all you're really doing is casting the TChar without the intent to change its value (and checked is slightly shorter).

@MihaZupan, `CreateChecked` should definitely not be preferred here just because the name is shorter.

`CreateChecked` has a lot more logic (making it tougher for the JIT to inline), explicitly uses `checked()` casts which can block some optimizations, and is meant explicitly for scenarios where an input is expected to throw. `CreateTruncating` is exactly what a normal cast would do and is preferred in all the cases where a normal cast would be used in non-generic code. It is smaller, simpler, easier to inline and optimize, etc.

More generally, we have an `IUtfChar<TSelf>` internal interface that provides some `CastFrom` methods specifically for doing the shared parsing logic and helping guarantee you get the most optimal handling possible and for outside corelib we've done something a bit like https://source.dot.net/#System.Runtime.Numerics/System/Number.Polyfill.cs,bcde44ac1f15f1ea to allow getting the same cheaper casts without needing to expose `IUtfChar` publicly.

I guess I was too optimistic to think that the JIT could handle a no-op `checked` for inline constants.
`CreateTruncating` is fine then to avoid this limitation.

review_comments: Previously this would have ended up with numberBase == Octal if current >= end. Now it'll end up as Decimal. I assume the stance is "that doesn't matter" because in both cases 0 means 0?

Yes, that's right. This would be triggered by any IPv4 address ending in .0, so I'd personally expect that to be treated as a base-10 octet in its own right (rather than an octal prefix with a missing digit) - but in reality, it makes no difference. Zero is zero in all three bases we support.
If this produces an error, but in the finally we then Free the native memory, will that end up corrupting whatever error code the caller might need to retrieve?

It won't on Windows: the documentation doesn't say that any of the methods changes the result of GetLastError, and testing confirms this - the return value is the only success/failure response, so there's no error code to corrupt. `SetLastError` was set to true on the interop definitions though, I've corrected this.

It will on Unix, so I've wrapped the Free in GetLastPInvokeError/SetLastPInvokeError as per the pattern in [CriticalHandle.Cleanup](https://github.com/dotnet/runtime/blob/main/src/libraries/System.Private.CoreLib/src/System/Runtime/InteropServices/CriticalHandle.cs#L149-L154).
